review_text_raw:
I have a confession.

I like goofy fake hacking scenes in movies.

I know it's not indicative of "actual" hacking, and as a programmer I should probably be a little miffed at how unrealistic they make the whole thing seem. But I don't care! I love it anyway.

Hacknet promised to give me that kind of feeling, and like Uplink before it, it kinda did. It's a puzzle game where your tools are 'hacking programs' and your problems relate to breaking into computers and grabbing info, deleting info, or causing chaos.

It works well, and it reveals just how satisfying it is to solve software problems, even when it's heavily abstracted and simplified.

But my biggest problem with Hacknet is that it never really takes that next step into something greater than a simplified hacking game. Toward the end of the game there's a distinct feeling of "That was it?"

Want to hack an SSH port? Then use SSHportHack.exe. Want to hack an FTP port? Then use FTPportHack.exe. The entire game is like this. For each problem or situation there's almost always exactly one answer, and there are few opportunities to feel clever. 

In some ways the game actually feels unfinished. Many computers you hack into contain generically named folders that are either empty or have snippets of IRC conversations from Bash.org. The game is set in modern times, yet your computer only has ~800mb of RAM and you can never upgrade it. The UI for selecting systems to hack into is an absolute nightmare.

There are even mechanics that don't seem to actually...exist? For example, a big deal is made about deleting your logs and leaving no trace behind - a classic hacking trope - yet I never once saw any consequences for forgetting. I eventually just stopped clearing logs and it never was a problem

As I said, I like Hackers-style hacking. It's fun and goofy and still scratches the same itch as actual hacking. Hacknet gets close, but its far too shallow and misses the mark.

review_text_raw:
I'm not entirely sure what the target demographic is for this game. It's an ostensibly terminal-based game running on a UNIX platform, but it has minimal overlap with bash commands, and trying to treat it like bash will only get you confused. 

So, this must be aimed at people without any tech background. However, how much fun can someone uninterested enough in coding to not care about this have, if all they're doing is typing in the same auto-completing commands over and over into a terminal?

Oh, and you can't scroll on the terminal, too. On the other hand, the GUI is both cluttered and unintuitive. Everything feels horrid to use.

It claims to feature "REAL HACKING", but the hacking consists of running magic hack spells via the terminal, and, if you DO know anything about hacking, that makes a lot of what the game asks of you feel obtuse. It took me so long to realise that I was supposed to open up a shell on my own PC, which, if crashed, would somehow take down a proxy server hosted elsewhere? I was assuming I had to find some kind of initial access mechanism to bypass the proxy and execute shellcode on the target PC, but, uh, I guess crashing the equivalent of cmd.exe on my computer really is the future of hacking.

The story is okay, I guess. At least it was easy to 100%.

My advice to anyone interested in a hacking-type game aimed at beginners is to check out the (free!) OverTheWire Bandit wargame, instead; it's fun, and it'll actually teach you something useful.

review_text_raw:
I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

review_text_raw:
PREFACE: I only played this game for one hour, and this may be a biased review, but so far I didn't see anything worth pursuing. The game may get interesting further down, but it just didn't pique my interesting so far.

This game does way too much hand holding to be enjoyable. If you're a casual gamer who wants to get the feeling that you're a cool hacker, go for it, but if you want any actual challenge, this game is not for you.

The whole game is just reading long emails trying to get the important information, then running the same sequence of commands over and over for every challenge. Every time they want to make it harder, they just add one more command to this sequence and repeat the same process.

There was very little problem solving or experimenting happening, which to me is what hacking is all about. Trying things out yourself and learning new tools. Not someone telling you what to do each step of the way.

The terminal interface was neat and the soundtrack was banging, but the game was just too bland and repetitive to be enjoyable.

review_text_raw:
[+] Soundtrack
[+] User Interface

[-] Plot
[-] World design and interaction

I bought this game mainly for its soundtrack, then because I'm a terminal guy myself and I love typing commands.
From this standpoint the game is beautiful: hastily keyboard mashing while listening to Gallego's killer tracks was awesome, not even mentioning the time when Carpenter Brut took over...

This game perfectly sets the mood for an awesome experience, with its music, its terminals and pseudo-graphical GUIs... but then falls short story-side.

[b]The plot is dull, linear and somewhat predictable.[/b]
You only have one bifurcation of the storyline that's even non-obvious to unlock. It gives you access to some more interesting missions, a new faction, and let you see a dark corner of the in-game Internet; but then it merges back into the main path in an abrupt way, as meaningless as it could get.
Yes, there are some interesting easter eggs and strange computer systems, but nothing that makes you want to explore on your own all that much.
There's only, like, [i]one[/i] moral choice, and it's not even part of the main quest.

[b]Whatever you do, whoever you damage, there's no consequence. The world simply doesn't react.[/b]
No cops backtracing you, no factions you can anger, no reputation system: you're part of the Good Guys from start to finish; you can screw up all the machines you want, you are The Savior and no one will change that.
Heck, you can even fail hacks and, apart from a panicking minigame to atone, no officer nor corporate killer will ever knock on your door.
You're simply bounced from a Good faction to another, without any chance to express your will. Just keep on hacking. Don't even bother to cover up your footprints. Logs are useless.

In the end, yes you can buy it, sure, but don't expect much except aesthetics.


[TECHNICAL NOTE]
The in-game console is backed by your native OS, and everything is deeply woven with its runtime.
Yes, you read it right.
That means two things:
[list]
    [*] if some of your game files break, you can be welcomed by an OS error printed on the console;
    [*] while this game runs on both Windows and Linux and has cloud sync, the save files are [b]not[/b] cross-platform; I suspect it has to do with different text encodings (save files are simple XMLs), and you need a repair tool you can find on the forums in order to convert them.
[/list]
Yeah, that wasn't nice.

review_text_raw:
This is an OK game. I wouldn't go as far as to compare it to either Uplink or the Street Hacker series simply because it feels more like a demo when compared to them. The execution and gameplay is shallow and naive. It's plagued by many basic design issues and most of the missions are just boring, repetitive, and feel more like a chore rather than a challenge.

My biggest gripes are:
-boring, repetitive and easy missions. Only 2 interesting missions stand out, the final Bit one, and the online pacemaker one.
-no sense of urgency or challenge. If you get caught hacking, that's just a reload to last checkpoint. No point in deleting any logs the way Uplink makes sure that you do. Uplink kept you on your toes because getting caught meant absolute game over!
-Badly designed UI. The workstation "map" is a cluttered mess especially as you move closer towards the end. Nodes are being randomly generated and the ones closest to the edge of the screen have their hover information cut off. How that ever went past the testers, I do not know!
-Weird writing, bad grammar, spelling mistakes, juvenile jokes scattered here and there. The ending was incredibly cheesy and anti-climactic.

Not a bad game to get on sale. But this is no Uplink for sure. The tagline shouldn't be "if you liked Uplink, you'll love this!" It's more the other way around because now I definitely feel like going back and replaying Uplink for the zillionth time! :)

review_text_raw:
Good: 
[list]
    [*]the command line UI is accurate, and makes you feel a lot like a real hacker.
    [*]nice music
    [*]lots of little easter eggs
    [*]technically very accurate (uses correct port numbers, IP addresses, and more)
[/list]

Bad: 
[list]
   [*]core gameplay is extremely repetitive and time consuming (which is an awful combination)
[/list]

The core gameplay of Hacknet revolves around you, a hacker, who can run several different programs to hack into a server and complete some task for a client. For example, hacking into the fried chicken chain CFC server and stealing the list of 11 secret herbs and spices.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. 

Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server.

At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment.

I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

review_text_raw:
I'd only recommend this game if: you get it for free or really cheap, you want a short game to play but don't care what, or you just really want to see lots of scrolling lines and feel like a faux hacker

Otherwise, I don't think it's worth your time for the following reasons:

1. too simple and repetitive
Once you figure out the command lines after a few minutes that's the entire game play. In fact, you'll have to type the same things over so many times you'll mostly use the GUI menu instead. Then, you just wait around all the time waiting for the same 4-5 port hacks to finish that's nothing more than progress bars and flashing numbers like you see in movies. You do this again and again over the next few hours doing simple contracts you pick up from the hacker group postings board (which don't require any thinking since they tell you exactly where to go and what to do which is most of the time just deleting some files off the target server). 

2. lack of story and immersion
As mentioned above, 90% of the time you are doing these simple job postings. The other 10% is the actual story but other than a quick introduction to the missing dead hacker in the beginning, all of its related missions are shoehorned at the end in like the last three missions. Also, another problem I had was the immersion. If you read the files in the folders they want you to target, they're related to the back story of the mission you're doing but if you poke around in the home folder they're just a bunch of random files. For example, it doesn't make sense to read irc chat logs of teenagers making dumb pun jokes and a grocery list in an enterprise server.

3. some poor ui choices
Every IP address you visit is pinned on a board as a node that you can revisit at anytime. However, the nodes become very cluttered towards the end of the game, and critical story nodes at the end are overlapped with a bunch of nodes you visited at the start of the game. I got stuck for a bit for one mission because when I scanned for connected networks I could not see the one out of the five that newly showed up which I needed to go to. It really didn't help that the countdown timer (active trace, which I'll talk about below) was right on top of that region, blocking my view. Lastly, there's something about the background and font color choice and or the font size that is eye straining and made me feel nauseous at times. Made me want to skim through the text a lot of the times.

4. feature bypass/abuse
There's a gameplay feature called active trace which is basically a countdown timer before the server tracks you down because it knows it's being hacked. Fun idea in theory but it's only ever a threat once in the game. Every other time you can circumvent it by hacking the server then disconnecting, then when you reconnect you can login as admin because it saved the password somehow from just hacking the ports. At this point you can leisurely scroll through the server and not worry about getting caught. If you do run out the timer and get caught you go into fail safe mode where you have a limited time to change your ip address but I just rebooted the virtual OS and that "solves" the problem.

The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

Just... bad. For anyone remotely familiar with computers, this game is cringe-worthy at best. Some weird mix of unix and dos idioms that just don't exist anywhere. - cd can't evaluate more than one step up or down the file tree

some other things to note:
- connections to other systems just don't make sense
- cracking ssh is somehow easier/less resource intensive than screwing with an ftp server? what?
- cat to read files?? really? I smell cat abuse
- no echo?

try again... or don't?

review_text_raw:
It is difficult to make a game that captures the feel of hacking. A hacker is successful because he has a large body of knowledge to pull from. He tries a thousand different things before something works.

Making an exciting game about hacking is like making an exciting game about coming up with new mathematical theorems. 

Hacknet is far more fun that I expected, but that isn't saying much. You are given four or five scripts to run with various levels of time pressure. There is a lot of good flavor, being able to customize your UI, using a simplified UNIX, and accessing system files.

Sadly, the gameplay wasn't enough to keep me playing and the story, while interesting, wasn't original enough to carry the game.

For a more detailed review of this and other Steam games I bought for cheap, check out my blog:

review_text_raw:
I have never left a review here in on steam for anything....that in itself should make you appreciate just how strongly I feel about what I am about to say and just how absolutely and unequivocally true what I am about to say really is.

Let's start from the positives.....actually positive:
The graphics are OK....along with the music it does create an atmosphere appropriate to the setting of the game.
That's it.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU BUY:
1) The game is essentially a mishap collection of dubiously formatted XML files, along with the main executable of the game which is obviously just a parser along with the graphics engine (presumably). Although it is possible to play the game normally, I guarantee that you will soon waste your time trying to "fix" the myriad of issues that arise from the poor structure of the gameplay itself (more on that later) See my play time? 87 hours? Most of it has been spent scouring the internet on ways to fix broken missions, enable progression through other parts of the story, etc.
2)There are several limits to and aspects of the basic design that make NO sense. For example, yes, you can use a "terminal" with a few commands to progress through the game. These commands include options to open and close your actual CD tray (wow, how ARG of the author--when was the last time anybody used the CD tray for anything? when was the last time anybody saw a computer with an actual CD drive ???). HOWEVER IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO CREATE OR DELETE DIRECTORIES IN YOUR IN-GAME COMPUTER, NOR CREATE FILES..That's right....as crazy as it sounds, you can't even copy files on your own machine. The only way to create files is downloading them from somewhere else and then renaming them if you want to "fake" a simple copy command....but yes, if you want a game that opens your CD tray by all means, stop reading this now and buy the game. The terminal itself has no ability to scroll up, which sometimes means you need to retrace your steps if you forgot to jot some key piece of information down.
3)There is no hardware upgrade system, which means your hacking machine is what it is from beginning to end. It doesn't really matter for the most part, as the speed of the operations you perform in the game is largely dependent on your own ability and response time (that's the main game mechanic). However RAM is kind of important, because that's what all your hacking tools consume to run, as expected. The problem is that if you, for example have the notes app open with passwords and information about your current mission (thus avoiding the aforementioned backtracking in point 2) , you will run out of memory pretty quickly...forcing you to run programs one at a time and wishing you could actually make money in this game to buy more than 1 GB of ram (lol...seriously...just lol).
4)You can only accept 1 mission at a time (WHY...JUST WHY?!???!). This may not seem a big issue, but it is what literally breaks the game again and again. This ridiculous limitation means that you can't complete all the missions offered in the game because no matter what you do as you progress through the story the game forces you to move on and leave the unfinished missions behind, never to be played. The only way to get past this is to go and edit your save game (you guessed it, an XML file) in order to make it possible to complete some missions (this fix doesn't always work btw). This becomes a huge problem close to the end of the story. Without spoiling anything, you end up having two missions to do, and it seems that it doesn't matter the order you do them in, but if you choose wrong a subsequent mission will be skipped entirely (it is one of the most notorious bugs of the game) and you will miss part of the narrative and context. Seriously, if you are thinking of buying this game, in order to enjoy the story as it was meant to be played, you should first look up what I have just told you and figure out which mission you should do first when you get to that juncture, or be prepared to restart the whole game if you mess up (unbelievable).
5)The least the author could've done was to include a save management system, but of course, there is none. If you want to make sure you don't have to restart the game in case something gets screwed up (see above) you must manually backup your savegame file, and you have to be careful too...because although the game doesn't autosave normally it will autosave in certain circumstances, barely warning you that this has been done.
6)Although the game never crashes, there are a few technical bugs that wouldn't even be a problem if not for everything that i mentioned above. When working with the terminal, using the arrow keys to edit a command sometimes doesn't work properly, and there are a few other such things (sometimes, for example, you have to hack a computer twice because although you were able to hack in the first time, the game doesn't register it). There are also a few grammar mistakes that again, not really important on its own but if added to all of the above, it's just the "cherry" on top that you don't want...especially from a paid game, however cheap it is. 
7) There is a ranking system, but it doesn't work. No matter how many missions you complete and how high your rank is according to the success emails you get at the end of each completed mission, you are still the last on the list, with 0 points. It's annoying. Suggestion to the author: if a feature is too hard/you are to lazy to implement...don't include it, especially if it has no bearing on the gameplay whatsoever. It is pretty disappointing to reach the end of the game and see that in the eyes of your hacking faction you are still a newb. 

Now....I get it, it's an indie game...what did I expect? Well I expected something a little more functional. As a software developer myself I understand a few of the choices the author made, but sill...there are some laps in basic human logic that are beyond me. For example, it is obvious that is technically more difficult to write an "open world" style game as opposed to a linear game play experience. That's why the player is allowed to play one mission at a time. I really get it. What I don't get is if a linear game is what you wanted to code...THEN DO NOT OFFER CHOICES TO THE PLAYER THAT YOUR GAME IS UNABLE TO SUPPORT AND FORCE HIM/HER/THEY TO START OVER!!!
I also understand that is hard to test a piece of software by yourself, I have done it as my main occupation for many years. A few bugs are bound to crop up...but hey...IN THE CREDITS THERE ARE MENTIONED A WHOLE SLEW OF TESTERS...what the heck did they test exactly? Seriously...I want to see what test cases they ran on this....

I would ask for a refund...but hey if didn't get my 60 bucks back from CD Projekt RED for Cyberprank 2077 I certainly won't ask the 5 bucks i spent on this (i got the DLC too). Go ahead, enjoy your Starbucks latte on me.  
According to the author, this game started out as a 48h game jam project and was later refined for 2 and a half years to become what's on steam now. 2/3 YEARS??!?!?! THIS IS WHAT YOU COME UP WITH? I think the best definition of this game is just that....a barely interesting project  hurriedly cobbled together  for a 48h game jam event.

tl;dr; Do yourself a favor and buy Uplink Elite, which is obviously what this game wanted to be and failed...miserably. I'd be willing to gift Uplink to the author as well so that he can see how a game like this SHOULD be made.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is the lone developer's pet project, and it saddens me to give it a negative rating. Honestly, though, I just didn't enjoy the game at all. It is extraordinarily repetitive, and after a while, it feels that you're doing nothing except waiting for hacking animations to finish. With only 2 exceptions, [i] every [/i] mission can be beaten by typing the same 6-7 commands in a predetermined order. After 2-3 hours of gameplay, I kept asking myself, "why is every mission the same, and why am I being forced to do it again and again?"

I did enjoy the jokes hidden in the IRC chat logs, but even then, they repeated themselves. If you read every IRC log in the game, you'd run across the same exact joke (literally) 4-5 times. It's a bit disappointing that the developer couldn't even populate the IRC logs with unique jokes. 

As an alternative criticism... the UI has some definite issues. For example, the node map gets so cluttered that it becomes completely unusable. You're constantly forced to backtrack and look at the mission statement in order to remind yourself which nodes should be broken into. It's very frustrating, and definitely killed my sense of immersion.

All in all, I can't recommend this game. I understand that others love it, but honestly, it just wasn't for me.

review_text_raw:
This game is good. Just not great.

I actually didn't finish this game, but I read a story synopsis and it was, well, not too creative. Decent, but not amazing. The reason I didn't finish is because the story effectively takes a break for about 8-10 hours after the first hour, having you invest into smaller stories that you come across in small missions. The other reason I didn't finish was that the gameplay felt like actual hacking and work, and it was the kind of grindy, difficult work that one might receive in a classroom. Some features of the UI were extremely difficult to operate, and while that was somewhat realistic, I came to play a game, not because I liked doing difficult computer work, which is part of the reason why some hackers become hackers. Speaking of that, this game makes hacking extremely easy and simplified. I guess that if a hacking OS was developed in real life, it may actually be this easy, but in reality now hacking is way more difficult, complicated and sometimes more fun than this.

The world building and details were fantastic. I can't tell you how many times I laughed scrolling through logs on PCs I'd hacked into. They were well written and funny. But the massive break from the story made me feel like I was actually doing hacker work (although way too easy) and not playing a game. I came to experience a story, play a game, be something and someone else for a while, not to actually do hacker work. This game did not advertise as a hacker sim, but as a game where you play as a hacker with a story. That is my main problem with this game.

And don't get me wrong--I am all about games that require you do think and reflect and do not have big visuals or explosions or gunfights--this game's gameplay was boring. I've already said how the hacking was too easy and the UI was way too hard, but simply, hacking got boring rather quickly. That's basically it. In terms of additional information, there were no bugs and it was programmed very solidly. 

Overall, get this game when it is very cheap and play it for a few hours. You can have more fun with it than just two hours, so you don't have to return it, just buy it very cheap or free, that's how I got this game, it was free for a limited time and I downloaded it. 79/100 -- good, just not a B.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a game about hacking. The game opens with the Hacknet OS booting up with a message from a man named Bit, who says that if you see the message, he’s already dead. He leads you on a quest to start hacking, getting the attention of one hacker group, then a second, all to avenge his death and prevent the distribution of a hacking program.

The story itself is kind of mediocre, but it is serviceable; at its core, it is a story of corporate greed, as well as a revenge story, though by the end of it, it is pretty clear that the whole thing isn’t really as sinister as it appeared at first.

The real core of the story is the hacking – you log into various computers, break through their security mechanisms, and then are lead onto other computers. Spicing things up are timers, various mechanisms you have to bypass, and the various files and passwords and IPs you have to find to lead you on the next leg of your hunt.

Sadly, the game is plagued with poor design decisions. There are various points at which it isn’t clear what you’re supposed to be doing, and you’re left confused, only to find out you needed to hit the “reply” button on an email after breaking into a server to move on – despite the fact that the email wasn’t clear about that. At other times, you have to send them messages, and while this is usually clear (sending them an IP or password), on occasion it is not and ends up being rather frustrating.

Worse (and even more frustrating) are some outright bugs – situations where the game simply does not function like it is supposed to. Beyond there being some lost forevers in the game which are less than obvious, there’s additionally the fact that sometimes the game simply bugs out and won’t let you progress or do various things. You get a “mission incomplete” message when trying to proceed, and there’s simply no clear way around the issue. Indeed, two of the achievements require you to do things which simply don’t function half the time or more, judging by the many frustrated players who had to restart the game time and again to try and get them to work.

The UI itself is a bit obtuse at times as well; several of the hacking programs you use require additional bits of typing to execute, despite the fact that in many cases it literally never matters – it is always exactly the same number you have to punch in. And while it is neat seeing it use actual hackerish commands, ultimately there’s a lot of little pieces which just feel annoying to have to do time and again.

The only real good thing about the game is its aesthetics; which do work pretty well for what it is.

In the end, you aren’t really rewarded for your frustration. The core idea is cute enough, but in the end the game ends up being rather repetitive, and there just isn’t enough variation in the core gameplay. A mediocre story combined with sometimes unclear gating mechanics to make the game advance is just not a winning recipe for a game.

The game seems like a neat idea at first, but it just ends up being more frustrating than enjoyable to play. It isn’t worth your time or your money.

I didn't enjoy this game much at all. I like the idea of playing a hacking simulator, but the execution really fell flat. The challenges are monotonous and uninteresting. Did you want to !solve because you didn't get everything you wanted the first time you broke in? Too bad.

Definitely not worth the price or your time.

Terribly disappointed by this game. Even the 3€ something during the most recent sale were too much, imho.

While the Game does use some Linux command line inputs to navigate on the computer (cd to change folders, ls to list contents, cat to read a file), those become useless once you completed the tutorial and gain access to the User Interface (mouse control), which is much faster.
"Hacking" works by starting skripts that automate the whole process. All you have to do is start the same 5 skripts by typing their name:
If there is a proxy active, use your own to overload it (click the overwhelm button).
If there is a firewall active, type analyze 5 times, then type solve and the password that was just revealed.
For any available port, type the name of the corresponding skript, wait for it to finish (about 10 seconds), then start the next one.
Sometimes, there is a time limit that never really got close to bothering me.

The story is either really weak or did not really start by the time I quit. You get a first E-Mail (I don't know you, please help me). Then, to build up your skills, you hack at least two dozen systems, always using the method described above, working your way up in some hacker organization you don't really know anything about. When you finally find that you are done with them, you start at bottom level of the next organization.

Conclusion:
Apart from my desire not to leave the game unfinished, there is absolutely nothing that would make me keep playing. Not recommended.

This game was a great idea with very poor followthrough. You learn two or three tricks to bypass security, have to collect the appropriate scripts to defeat each of the half dozen interfaces, and then boom, you're a legendary hacker. It's all text-based with a super basic linuxy command line interface, which I'm sure makes some people feel like they're all h4xx0r... I'm probably being unnecissarily harsh, but I really was shocked at how repetative this game was. 

It seemed like there were alot of mechanics that they planned, but never got around to implementing. All that hype about deleting the logs after you access a computer... maybe I missed something, but I couldn't see that it did anything. And the Trap and Forkbombs... were those actually useful somehow? Oh, and it was very easy to make game-breaking mistakes, like deleting a file you were supposed to steal. Alot of silent ways to ruin the game and be unable to recover... hope you didn't save after one of those.

There are alot of fun points. Getting a new script and seeing the new computers you can crack is exciting. The story in the beginning and end of the game are interesting. Also the little easter-eggs of emails and chat snippets were pretty funny. And I'm sure the game does look cool if you let people see you playing it. 

My background in embedded sofware may have colored my opinion a bit, but the game felt awfully thin for $10. And from a gameplay perspective, it was awfully rough. Serious programmers should look at TIS-100 instead, although beware: Zacktronics games are not for the faint-hearted, and may feel a little too much like work to the professional programmer.

review_text_raw:
There is no overarching narrative; you're completing puzzles with no purpose. 

Thus, the puzzles are the focus of the game. However, the puzzles are simple and boring. Simple puzzles can still be interesting. Imagine a child's toy where you fit shapes through their respective holes. You can keep yourself busy for a little bit. This game is similar, but everything is a square. How many times can you fit the square in the square hole before it gets boring? Example: you need the password to decrypt a file and you'll find it on the same system within a file called "password.txt". 

Firewall solving requires no input from the player, it's just a timesink. You call the "analyze" command and wait a few seconds at a time until it reveals the answer. You need to call this command multiple times before it starts to reveal the answer - what gameplay function does this serve? Sometimes you don't have any other task to do while the analyze command is processing, so you just wait and wait.. like an idle game. 

Overloading a proxy server involves clicking a button and waiting a few seconds (depending on the number of shells you have up). There's no depth.

Missions share objectives in the form of notes on your computer. For some reason, the devs thought it was a bright idea to have notes take up a significant portion (~30% sometimes) of your memory. So you often have to write up your own abbreviated notes or you won't have enough memory to run the programs you need to crack the ports. The game is fighting itself.

The UI is a mess. A couple hours and your network map becomes an unintelligible mess with no tools to label systems or otherwise organize it. Missions could at least highlight linked servers.

The music is repetitive. Music can make or break a game. In this case, I found myself shutting off music to play my own playlist in the background so I wouldn't be bored to tears while doing all of the waiting the game requires.

review_text_raw:
1. You can't finish all contracts. At some point the game will just tell you "You're good enough for more difficult tasks" and a main quest will trigger, blocking you from accepting new quests. You can never go back and you can't do them after the final mission.

2. You can't create files or directories. Organizing your downloaded files is annoying because you can only use the pre-defined ones. In one contract you're supposed to forge a file, and that works by downloading a file and editing the copy...

3. You can't remove directories. There's almost never a need to do so, but when you need to remove the contents from a directory with multiple subdirectories, you need to access each subdir individually and remove the contents.

4. Autocomplete doesn't add a whitespace after the autocompleteted word. Confusing as hell for a regular terminal user.

5. The final mission consists of multiple phases, which each one explaining your next goal. In phase 3 you're supposed to send a password but you aren't told so. I just used the password I found to login and continued my quest. After a while I got stuck, and after more than an hour I finally looked into a walkthrough - and learnt that I needed to send the password instead of entering it, and that had already solved the final mission by myself over an hour ago. At least I could just click the "complete quest" button 4 times in a row to trigger the ending.

6. The gameplay is quite repetetive. Connect to a server, open the closed ports (which always works the same, for all of them), find the file you need. There are only 2 missions that go beyond that and actually force you to think: The final mission, and the mission before. That doesn't really speak for the game.

7. The map is just plain awful. It's cluttered with nodes from earlier contracts which you never need to connect to anymore. Literally hardest part of the game is finding the correct node on the map.

8. Secrets. Don't get me wrong, secrets are great. But I looked into a guide after finishing the game, and some secrets didn't trigger for me although I definitely satisfied their conditions. So maybe I shouldn't have written "Secrets", but "Bugs". Furthermore, some secrets get you hyped, and when you finally solve their puzzle, you get... a digital clock that even uses up your RAM?

9. Alt+Tab closes the game.

I completed the game in a single session. It was kinda fun, although way too easy. But damn, some of the issues I just mentioned are pissing me off and I'm not going to play the DLC or any user-created mod.

Oh, and step away from it for a few days, and you'll forget everything you need to do each step of the game. You can take notes, but the game penalizes you for that by having the notes app take up a ridiculous amount of memory. The story and the text seem okay, some of it super tropey, others of it genuinely surprising. There is some branching, but it was not enough to really carry me forward. TLDR; A great game, a great concept, that was too much like an actual job to be fun.

To be fair Uplink is better. This game is good because you get to use the keyboard. Uplink is a hacking game where keyboard is not used, so the biggest flaw is now solved. Problem is the game lacks a bit of adrenaline. 

1) Most servers don't trace you, so you can just hang around forever.
2) Its not clear where you are connected too. Once you hack a place is there opened forever. You don't even have to disconnect.
3) You clear your logs but not the disconnected log, which makes no sense. In Uplink you have to clear logs at origin and destination, seems more realistic.
4) Its too easy to go up the ranking. 
5) In Uplink you had money to worry about. Upgrade hardware and buy software. In Hacknet all you get is reputation, that also have no impact besides gettings invitations.
6) The game does not allow you to accept more than 1 mission.
7) The storyline is a bit broken. I made 1 mission that lead to a hacker invading my computer, that leads to another mission and to another mission and basically you cannot accept other mission while the "story" is leading you in 1 way. That made me join an organization and now I cannot finish the old missions. Basically I lost 3 missions, cannot be played.
8) The game UI is a bit limited. I cannot open a file and an email at the same time. Which makes very annoying to take note to things. Althought I cannot complain much on that, as in Uplink I really had a pen and paper next to me all the time, in this game I never used real paper so far.
9) Uplink allow you to do other stuff, such as Stock Market, browse any server, etc. Hacknet is limited. You only get the servers IP when the game wants you to get. There is not freedom besides follow the story.
10) Uplink allows you to choose which mission to make, in the sense of choosing to be a good or a bad hacker. In Hacknet some missions presentation don't have more than 2 lines. You have to accept missions without even knowing what skills you need, what tools you need and what you have to do. Its really 1 path only. And if you try to get missions in different orders you lose them, just like I lost 3. UPDATE: Because of this 1 path only + cannot accept more than 1 mission, you can game over all the time. If you delete the wrong file, edit the wrong record, its finished. People call this bug in the forum, I call this lack of flexibility. In Uplink you could simply give up on a mission and pay a fine. If you delete a file you are suppose to upload, it shouldn't be game over, just some kind of punishment.
11) It uses Unix commands but limit them. For instance you have rm command but cannot be used to delete folders. Cannot download folders either.
12) Find it a bit weird that no special software is required to know when you are being traced.
13) So far the challenge of the game seems to be more about curiosity of the player. Meaning you have to look into every folder and file and read and see what you can find (be aware) rather than having a challenge on the hacking it self, such as limited time, required software, go throught LAN networks, etc.
14) You can hack a webserver, a main frame, a home pc or a cell phone, they all look the same, they all have same file structure, they are all hacked with same tools. A bit boring no?
15) Network map completely unecessary. Its just a harder way to find servers, if you are not going to use it to bounce like Uplink, why have that? Just a window with animated blue balls. A list with a search box and some favorites would do the job, or better, connect always using the line command, IP or name assigned by the user.
16) Once you scan a server and it reveals other computers connected to that, more "balls" appears and its a mystery why some are very distant and some are very close. The distance is based on what? It simple confuses the player as it adds a connection between them and with time the connections cross each other. Well, still trying to figure out why did it this way.
17) I'm already playing this game for hours and all I do is execute programs to open ports.


The good:

a) Very well done interface in the sense that keyboard and mouse usage is well integrated. The key here is keyboard. Its very nice to be able to play the entire game using keyboard only.
b) I like the fact that webserver have website with real images. Just because its a hacker game, it doesn't mean the "normal" internet doesn't exist. Although limited, I liked the www.cfc.com.
c) You can see an effort to bring interesting content to see around. Most servers have files that are not crucial to the missions, things you can read, chats, funny stuff. That really adds to the game and was one of the things I feel lacking in Uplink. Perhaps this is one of the reason a lot of servers don't have tracing mechanism, so you don't have time pressure all the time.
d) Not having time pressure all the time is good, but also removed money pressure and other stuff, which is left it a bit unbalanced.
e) Nice animations. The screens change a lot. Its not the same interface all the time.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What to expect if you're new to this game genre[/h1]
Hacknet is a new title in the otherwise stagnant, indie genre of hacking simulation games.
And a fresh breeze it is.

No doubt there is hardly any competition for this kind of quality.
Graphics are amazing, the hacking system introduced is quite good and consistent, it has gigantic potential for expansion that desperately needs to be used, and hopefully will. In it's current shape there might be little room for multiplayer gameplay, because of the game mechanics, but hopefully as the game gets finalized it will be implemented.

The puzzles you have to face are fun to solve and most of the time at medium or easy difficulty level.
Even though the game description provided on Steam might be a little misleading, as to non-holywood hacking style, or minimal hand-holding, the gameplay can be extremely exciting and satisfying.
The thrill of hacking, taking unauthorised control over websites, other web services, or user machines and mobile devices, identity theft or destruction, and constantly racing the trace clock are all very satisfying and will give you an addictive adrenaline rush.

Music is a very proper and enjoyable background for your virtual crimes, not quite something to remember.

The game has too high hardware requirements in my opinion. All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!)

[h1]Finally the 'Uplink vs Hacknet'[/h1]
Many people look up to Hacknet in comparison to Uplink.
Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy.
The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging.
If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding.
Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet.

[h1]Final words[/h1]
Whatever Hacknet is or will be, I'd say Uplink is worth playing, as the only other hacking game out there with some serious gameplay to this date.
If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers.
Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

review_text_raw:
Got the game for free and it has been sitting in my backlog for a while. Some while ago I finally decided to clear this game with high expectations seeing it receive a lot of positive reviews. Unfortunately I was faced with only disappointment.

At first the gameplay is intriguing and engaging. The terminal style UI certainly looks cool. There are quests that procedurally guide you through the mechanics of the game, and the discovery process keeps the gameplay fresh, but not for long until you join the hacker organization.

From that point what you do is just repeating the same hacking routine again and again, and it gets repetitive very quickly. At this point the only thing left that can do some good for this game is the story. My last hope for the game was that after hours of labour I would uncover traces of a big conspiracy that leads me to something like stopping a skynet, or fighting myself in a moral conflict, you get the meaning.

But no! The main plot is linear and doesn't have much depth to it. It was so uninspiring that I didn't even know I came to the end of the story, just after I did the usual hacking stuff I was greeted with a voice recording and I was like "is that it?".

Also the 'hacking experience' is far from realistic. But I guess it serves the point of letting people feel like they're a hacker.

I really want to like this game, but I couldn't. The music is good though, I think it's the only plus side.

TL;DR: Cool hacking-look UI, repetitive hacking routine, weak story

This game seems OK, but it seems very repetitive.

The general UI is pretty good, with both a text and graphical interface. There doesn't seem to be any support for commands that would let you write scripts that might help to automate some of the repetitive actions - having to type out each of the actions you need to take when theres a count down timer is annoying.

The UI seems to be quite unresponsive / laggy, which is odd considering it is very basic. Sometimes clicks or key presses don't register.

I do like the way the interface acts like a machine though, such as requiring certain modules like the x server in order to work.

However, I just dont like the repetitive nature, and can't really recommend it.

What you're paying for here is a really fancy UI. Gameplay isn't that deep, it mostly consists of typing a few characters and pressing tab to autocomplete. There's a game mechanic where you're encouraged to delete logs detailing your activity while you're inside another person's computer, but at the end of the day, it doesn't matter because there are no real fail-states in this game. It's super casual. The soundtrack is okay, I guess.
